title: #17 Be aware of Wait Time 2
author: Craig Barton
summary: The seventeenth Tips for Teachers newsletter, and the second half of a pair on wait time. Where the previous issue covered the gap between question and response, this one addresses the less-discussed second wait time: the pause between a student answering and the teacher making the next move. Barton's image for it is letting a student's answer hang in the air. He cites Mary Budd-Rowe's claim that extending this second pause to at least three seconds produces four benefits - peers compare the answer to their own, behaviour and attention improve, student-to-student exchange increases, and teachers make better use of responses. The tip has two halves, and the second is the one teachers usually miss: lengthening the silence is not enough, because research on self-explaining shows most students will not use the time spontaneously. Barton's line is that without a prompt students will simply look at you like a buffering YouTube video, so he supplies explicit comparison questions to give the silence a task. The physical cue he uses to lengthen the pause is tapping three seconds out on his leg.
points: The distinction between the two wait times is the whole point - most teachers who have heard of wait time only ever extend the pause before the answer, not the one after it.
Barton's practical mechanism is physical rather than cognitive: tapping three seconds on his leg after a response, because the pause will not happen by intention alone.
The self-explaining research supplies the caveat that makes the tip work - silence is inert unless students are told what to do with it, since most will not self-explain naturally.
The prompt he gives is specific and repeatable: how does this answer compare to mine, what is the same and what is different.
The claimed payoff runs beyond learning into behaviour and classroom dynamics, with Budd-Rowe's list including improved attention and more student-to-student exchange.
quotes: Last week, we discussed the importance of increasing the time between asking students a question and calling upon them to respond. In the research world, this is called wait time.

But there is another wait time we need to be aware of: the time between students sharing an answer and us making our next move. I think of this as the opportunity to let a student's answer hand in the air.

There are two important factors we need to consider here. The first is actually increasing this second type of wait time. Like last week, I find the technique of tapping our 3 seconds on my leg after a student responds to be effective.

But we must also encourage our students to make the most of this time. Research into self-explaining suggests that the majority of students do not do it naturally. If we just let an answer hang in the air, our students may look at us like we are a YouTube video that is buffering.
So we may need to prompt them to reflect silently on their peer's response: How does this answer compare to mine? What is the same and what is different?
